about: Overview

Solicitors in England and Wales can pay introducers for client introductions in most areas of work, provided they follow the rules that apply to referral arrangements. Those rules come mainly from the SRA Standards and Regulations, including the SRA Principles and the Code of Conduct, and from the Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act 2012, often called LASPO, which bans referral fees in certain kinds of work.

This page explains, in general terms, how those rules usually apply to a firm that pays an introducer such as Leaflegal, and how our service is set up with them in mind. It is general information, not regulatory advice. Every firm's position is different, the rules and the SRA's guidance can change, and your compliance officer is the right person to take a view on any arrangement your firm enters into.

Leaflegal is an introduction service run by Vertical Brands Ltd. It is not a law firm, is not regulated by the SRA and does not give legal advice. It runs campaigns, asks people a short set of questions about their matter and, with their consent, introduces each one to a single partner firm. Firms pay Leaflegal for each introduction at a price agreed in advance.

about: Referral arrangements are an area the SRA has looked at closely over the years. A firm that gets them wrong can face regulatory consequences, and clients who feel misled about how they were introduced can lose trust in the firm. Getting them right is not difficult, but it does need attention.
Telling clients

Transparency is at the heart of the rules on introducers. In general terms, the SRA Code of Conduct requires firms to make sure that clients are told about any financial or other interest that an introducer has in referring them, and about any fee sharing arrangement that is relevant to their matter. Fee sharing arrangements are required to be in writing.

Before anyone can submit an enquiry, they tick a box confirming they understand Leaflegal is an introduction service, not a law firm. Our consent wording explains that Leaflegal is paid by the firms it introduces people to. We record the exact wording and the time the client agreed to it, and we send that record with every lead.

Most firms mention the introduction on the first call, for example by saying the client made an enquiry through Leaflegal and asked to speak to a solicitor. Many then confirm the referral arrangement in writing, usually in the client care letter, so there is a clear record. The wording you use, and how much detail you give, is a matter for your firm and your compliance officer.

about.h3: Matching what the client was told

about: Having our consent wording with each lead makes it easier for your own client care information to match what the client has already been told. A client who reads the same message from Leaflegal and from your firm is far less likely to be confused or concerned about how they came to you.

Firms generally aim to tell clients about a referral arrangement at the outset, before the client is committed. Mentioning it on the first call and confirming it at the point of engagement is a common approach. Your compliance officer can confirm what your firm expects.

Whatever approach your firm takes, keep a record that the client was told. The consent record that comes with each Leaflegal lead shows what the client was told before they enquired. Your own file note of the first call and your client care letter show what your firm told them. Together they give a clear picture if anyone later asks how the client came to you.
Independence
The SRA Principles require solicitors to act with independence and in the best interests of each client. A referral arrangement must not get in the way of either.

An introducer should not be able to influence the advice a firm gives, the way it runs a matter or the fees it charges. The client should be free to instruct the firm or not, and free to go elsewhere at any time. The firm's professional judgement must remain its own.

Leaflegal makes the introduction and then steps back. We do not tell clients which firm to choose beyond the introduction itself. We do not comment on the merits of their matter, the likely outcome or what they should do. We have no say in the advice you give, the work you do or the fees you agree with the client. We do not receive any share of your fees. We are paid for the introduction at a price agreed in advance.

Your price per lead does not depend on whether the client instructs you or on the fees you earn from the matter. A lead stays valid if the client chooses another firm or decides not to proceed. That separation helps keep the introduction and the legal work apart.

Exclusive introductions mean Leaflegal introduces each client to one firm. That does not limit the client's freedom. They can choose not to instruct your firm and can approach any other firm on their own. Firms should respect that choice and never pressure a client to instruct.

Many firms carry out their own checks on any introducer they work with, looking at how clients are found, what they are told and how their data is handled. We are happy to answer those questions and show you our consent wording before you sign anything.
Banned fees
Some referral fees are banned outright by law, regardless of how well an arrangement is disclosed.

Section 56 of the Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act 2012 prohibits the payment and receipt of referral fees in relation to claims for damages for personal injury or death, which includes clinical negligence claims. Leaflegal does not generate personal injury or clinical negligence enquiries in any form. People with those matters are told we cannot help before they submit an enquiry.

Some kinds of claim, such as financial mis-selling claims, involve regulated claims management activity, which is overseen by the Financial Conduct Authority. Leaflegal does not handle financial claims or housing disrepair claims. Our seven practice areas are conveyancing, family law, immigration, debt recovery for businesses, licensing, lease extensions and trademarks.

The SRA has made clear over the years that it looks at the substance of an arrangement rather than its label. A payment described as a marketing fee or an administration charge can still be treated as a referral fee if that is what it really is. This matters most in areas where referral fees are banned, which is one reason Leaflegal stays out of those areas entirely.

Our form filters out personal injury and clinical negligence matters, but clients do not always describe their situation accurately. If a lead you receive turns out to involve a personal injury claim, do not treat it as a Leaflegal introduction for that work, and let us know straight away. Your partner agreement sets out how such a lead is handled.

about.h3: Areas we chose to leave out

about: Leaflegal's choice of practice areas reflects these rules. We generate enquiries only in areas where paying an introducer is permitted, subject to the other rules on this page, and we have chosen to stay out of claims work altogether. If you would like us to cover an area we do not currently offer, mention it on your call, but we will not add any area where referral fees are banned.
Other limits
Beyond disclosure and the LASPO ban, the SRA Code contains further restrictions that firms need to consider when using any introducer.

The Code restricts firms from making payments to an introducer in respect of clients who are the subject of criminal proceedings. For that reason Leaflegal does not generate enquiries from people facing criminal proceedings. If a criminal matter comes up during your first call with a client, deal with it under your own arrangements and do not treat it as part of the introduction.

The Code also restricts payments to an introducer in respect of clients who have the benefit of public funding. Every Leaflegal client confirms they want paid legal help rather than legal aid or free advice before their enquiry is submitted. If a client you speak to turns out to be publicly funded for the matter, consider the position carefully and let us know.

Firms are expected to make sure that clients referred by an introducer were not obtained in a way that would breach the SRA's rules if the introducer were regulated by the SRA. That includes rules against unsolicited approaches to members of the public. Leaflegal does not cold call, buy data or scrape directories. Every client found us through our own campaigns and asked to be introduced.

Firms are responsible for making sure publicity about their services is accurate and not misleading. Leaflegal runs its campaigns under its own name and does not advertise partner firms by name. We do not present ourselves as a law firm.

Leaflegal is not regulated to give immigration advice and does not do so. Immigration enquiries go only to firms regulated by the SRA or CILEx Regulation, or to advisers registered with the Immigration Advice Authority at the right level for the work.

faqs: The basics
Can solicitors pay for client referrals?

In most areas of work, yes, as long as they follow the rules on referral arrangements. Clients must be told about the arrangement, the firm's independence must not be compromised and referral fees must not be paid where they are banned, such as personal injury. This is general information. Your compliance officer can confirm how the rules apply to your firm.
Is Leaflegal regulated by the SRA?

No. Leaflegal is an introduction service, not a law firm, and is not regulated by the SRA. We do not give legal advice. That is made clear to every client before they submit an enquiry. The professional relationship, and the regulatory duties that come with it, sit with your firm.
Is paying per lead a referral fee?

Firms should assume that paying an introducer for introductions is a referral arrangement and treat it as one, including telling clients about it. The SRA looks at the substance of an arrangement rather than what it is called. Your compliance officer can take a view on how your arrangement with Leaflegal is treated.
Where do the referral rules come from?

Mainly from the SRA Standards and Regulations, which include the SRA Principles and the Code of Conduct, and from section 56 of the Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act 2012, which bans referral fees in personal injury work. The SRA also publishes guidance on referral fees and introducers.
Does this page count as regulatory advice?

No. It is general information about how referral rules usually work and how Leaflegal is set up. It is not advice on your firm's position. The rules and guidance can change, so check the current versions and speak to your compliance officer before entering into any referral arrangement. We can explain the facts.
Do the same rules apply to CILEx and CLC firms?

CILEx Regulation and the Council for Licensed Conveyancers have their own codes, which include rules on referrals and introducers. The principles are broadly similar, including transparency with clients, but the detail differs. If you are regulated by one of them, check their current rules and guidance. The same goes for the IAA.
Does the SRA publish guidance on referral fees?

Yes. The SRA has published guidance over the years on referral fees, introducers and the LASPO ban. It is worth reading the current versions on the SRA website, because guidance can be updated. Your compliance officer will usually be familiar with it and can explain how it applies to your firm.
Disclosure
Do I need to tell clients about Leaflegal?

Yes. In general terms, the SRA Code of Conduct requires you to make sure clients are told about any financial arrangement you have with an introducer. Most firms mention it on the first call and confirm it in writing, usually in the client care letter. Your compliance officer can confirm your firm's approach.
What have clients already been told?

Every client confirms they understand Leaflegal is an introduction service, not a law firm, and our consent wording tells them that Leaflegal is paid by the firms it introduces. We record the exact wording and the time they agreed to it, and send that record with every lead. You can show this to your compliance officer.
Do I need to tell clients how much I pay?

Firms take different approaches to how much detail they give, and the rules and guidance should be checked for your firm's position. Many firms explain the nature of the arrangement clearly. Your compliance officer can advise on what your firm should say in its client care information. Make it consistent across your firm.
When should I tell the client?

Firms generally aim to tell clients at the outset, before the client is committed to instructing them. A common approach is to mention it on the first call and confirm it in writing at the point of engagement. Our consent wording means the client has already been told once, before they ever speak to you.
Does Leaflegal's consent wording replace my disclosure?

No. It helps, because the client has already been told that Leaflegal is paid by the firms it introduces, but your own duty to make sure clients are told remains. Use our wording as a starting point so that your client care information matches what the client has already seen.
Should I mention Leaflegal on the first call?

It usually helps. Saying the client made an enquiry through Leaflegal and asked to speak to a solicitor tells them straight away that the call is expected. It is also a natural moment to mention the referral arrangement, before confirming it in writing. Clients sometimes forget the name of the service they used, so mentioning it helps them place the call. A short file note of what you said gives your firm a record.
Is there a fee sharing arrangement with Leaflegal?

Leaflegal does not take a share of your fees. We are paid a price per lead agreed in advance, which does not depend on whether the client instructs you or what you charge them. How your compliance officer classifies the arrangement for disclosure purposes is a matter for your firm.
Restricted areas
Why don't you offer personal injury leads?

Paying referral fees for personal injury and clinical negligence work is prohibited under section 56 of the Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act 2012. Leaflegal does not generate those enquiries in any form, and people with those matters are filtered out before they submit. This includes clinical negligence.
What if a lead turns out to involve personal injury?

Do not treat it as a Leaflegal introduction for that work, and tell us straight away. Our form filters out personal injury and clinical negligence, but clients do not always describe their situation accurately. Your partner agreement sets out how such a lead is handled. Prompt reporting helps us fix the cause.
What about clients with legal aid?

The Code restricts payments to introducers in respect of clients with the benefit of public funding. Every Leaflegal client confirms they want paid help, not legal aid or free advice. If a client turns out to be publicly funded for the matter, consider the position carefully and let us know.
Do you handle claims management work?

No. Financial mis-selling claims and similar work involve regulated claims management activity overseen by the Financial Conduct Authority. Leaflegal stays out of those areas, and out of housing disrepair claims, and focuses on privately paid work in our seven practice areas. People with those matters are told we cannot help before they submit, so they never become leads. Our seven areas are listed on our partner pages.
Finding clients
Do you cold call people?

No. Leaflegal does not cold call, buy data, rent lists or scrape directories. Every client found us through our own campaigns on social media, search or content, completed our enquiry form and asked to be introduced to a firm. We do not make unsolicited approaches to the public. Every client chose to fill in our form and ticked a separate box agreeing to be contacted by a firm about their matter.
Why does it matter how clients were obtained?

Firms are expected to make sure clients referred by an introducer were not obtained in a way that would breach the SRA's rules if the introducer were regulated, including rules on unsolicited approaches to the public. Knowing how an introducer finds clients is part of sensible due diligence. We are happy to answer questions.
Do you advertise my firm by name?

No. Our campaigns run under the Leaflegal name. We do not advertise partner firms by name or present ourselves as a law firm. The client learns your firm's name when you contact them. This keeps the introduction clear. When you call, introduce your firm and explain that the client made an enquiry through Leaflegal and asked to speak to a solicitor about their matter.
Can I see your consent wording before I sign?

Yes. We show you a sample lead on your call, including the consent record, so you and your compliance officer can see exactly what clients agree to. We are happy to answer questions about how enquiries are generated and filtered. Your compliance officer is welcome to review it, along with your partner agreement, before your firm commits to anything.
Do clients know they are being introduced to a law firm?

Yes. Every client ticks a separate box agreeing that their details can be shared with a firm we match them with, and that the firm can contact them by phone, email or text about their matter. They also confirm they understand that Leaflegal itself is not a law firm. The wording is recorded.
Independence
Does Leaflegal influence my advice?

No. Leaflegal makes the introduction and steps back. We do not comment on the merits of the client's matter, tell them what to do or have any say in your advice, the work you do or the fees you charge. Your duty to act in the client's best interests is unaffected by how they came to you. The advice, the work and the fees are matters for your firm alone.
Do you take a share of my fees?

No. Leaflegal is paid for each introduction at a price agreed in advance. Our price does not depend on whether the client instructs you or on the fees you earn from the matter. A lead stays valid if the client chooses another firm or decides not to go ahead. That separation helps keep the introduction and the legal work apart.
Can a client still choose another firm?

Yes. Exclusive introductions mean Leaflegal introduces each client to one firm only, but the client remains free to instruct you or not and to approach any other firm. Respecting that choice is part of acting in the client's best interests. Firms should never pressure a client to instruct them because of how they were introduced.
Who is responsible for compliance with the Code?

Your firm is responsible for its own compliance, including disclosure, independence, conflicts, client care and data protection. Leaflegal is responsible for how it finds clients, what it tells them and how it handles their data. We set the service up to support your duties, but we cannot carry them for you.
What about immigration advice?

Leaflegal is not regulated to give immigration advice and never does. Immigration enquiries go only to firms regulated by the SRA or CILEx Regulation, or to advisers registered with the Immigration Advice Authority at the right level for the work. All advice comes from the regulated firm or adviser. We never assess eligibility.
Does Leaflegal tell clients which firm is best?

No. Leaflegal matches each enquiry to one firm whose practice areas, matter types and locations it fits, and introduces the client to that firm. We do not rank firms, recommend one firm over another or comment on a firm's quality to the client. The client decides for themselves whether to instruct the firm after speaking to it.
